speaker: randwallis
text: All right, good morning and welcome to an oral argument session of the 5th District Court of Appeal. My name is Rand Wallace, I'll be presiding over these oral arguments today. The first one is the Serrano, I'm sorry, it's the Brevik versus State of Florida case. I want to introduce the other members of the panel. Joining me today is Judge Dan Traver from our court and from Orange County. And we also have, for the first time as a district court judge on our court, we want to welcome Judge Mary Alice Nardella to her first oral argument. And it's a privilege and an honor to preside over these oral arguments that is her first. And I also want to ask the parties if when you're giving your oral argument, make sure that you don't have any noise-making devices on the background that may interrupt your argument. I'm going to assume that the appellant wants five minutes in rebuttal, unless you tell me otherwise, and that's really all the instructions. So with that, we have Brevik versus the State of Florida, and counsel, you may proceed.

speaker: matthewmclain
text: Good morning, Matt McLean on behalf of the appellant, David Brevik. I will reserve the five minutes for rebuttal. May it please the court. There's several issues briefed today. To begin with, this was a highly technical case which involved the battle of the experts as to cause of death of Mrs. Brevik. One of the big issues from the state's expert was that the lack of-

speaker: traver
text: Good morning. Can I interrupt you before you get to that? Because there is just a general issue that I'm having with deficient performance in this case, and I'm wondering if in addressing first that second issue and whatever else that you deem fit, that you would consider that challenge that I'm having. Forgive me if it takes a second to frame my question because it's kind of fact intensive. I've never really seen a case like this, 86 days from arrest to trial on a case where initially the state pursued the death penalty and then dropped it after your client made his demand. It looks like they disclosed five experts, called two. I agree with you that it was medically intensive. Three private lawyers with about 90 combined years of trial experience, led by a board certified lawyer who did all the medical work. There is, I'm sure you're familiar, a Florida Supreme Court case named Maxwell, which basically talks about deficient performance, and I don't want to misquote it. The fact that a more thorough or detailed presentation could have been made does not establish an effective assistance of counsel. It is almost always possible to imagine a more thorough job being done than was actually done. So, the challenge I'm having with deficient performance, especially in light of what the trial court deemed a reasonable strategic decision not to waive speedy and rush towards trial in 86 days on a very intensive case where your client was able, through the help of many skilled counsel, to be able to retain multiple medical experts on short notice. I've just never seen anything like it. So I wondered if, in light of that long windup, if you could address deficient performance for me.

speaker: matthewmclain
text: There's no question that defense counsel for Mr. Brett did a lot of good things. They did hire three experts. They did present a good defense. However, that doesn't make up for the fact that they missed very important details. And when you have a state expert basically gutting your entire defense by saying, look, here are the brain slides, and no defense expert looked at them, and why is that when a cocaine overdose would be represented in the brain slides through brain tissue infarction, you have to address it. It completely gutted the defense in every which way.

speaker: traver
text: Was your client's trial counsel aware in advance that Dr. Kaiser would be testifying that way as it related to infarction?

speaker: matthewmclain
text: So at the evidentiary hearing, the defense attorney testified that he was not aware of it. He confessed to him that he knew it was false, but his expert had testified out of order. So he was caught off guard according to his evidentiary hearing testimony.

speaker: traver
text: But in that way, in your initial brief, you discuss that he should have raised the discovery violation in that instance, correct?

speaker: matthewmclain
text: Absolutely. If the state expert failed to testify in deposition or provided in his report that brain tissue infarction was going to be such an important detail, then any reasonable counsel would object to that and assert a discovery violation and seek remedial measures.

speaker: traver
text: Let's assume for a second that the trial judge would not have exercised the most extreme remedy under Richardson and caused Dr. Kaiser not to be able to testify at all. The next most extreme remedy would be, hey, you get a continuance to depose this expert, get back Dr. Bonfiglio and continue the trial. How do we view that though, in light of trial counsel's decision when offered with exactly that same remedy in the context of alleged Miranda violations to file a motion to suppress specifically, reasonably, and strategically discarded that particular remedy?

speaker: matthewmclain
text: So I guess that relates back to the part two or part one of the defense strategy, but related to the statement of particulars and the reason why they asserted the speedy trial and the demand for that. A continuance would not have resulted in that waiver of that issue. I think the second remedy would have been the proper remedy for the court to do under the circumstance, and the jury still would have been sworn in and the argument would not have been waived in any way by seeking a continuance and getting an expert to testify to what, at the evidentiary hearing, the defense counsel testifies is really important. He said that whatever the medical examiner says is important to a jury. The jury takes a lot of consideration to what that point is going to be. So certainly, when something so important comes up and you have nothing to combat it, you have to take some sort of action, and here, if we take true what defense counsel said at the evidentiary hearing, he did nothing. He didn't assert any sort of discovery violation, and so that issue never came up. Instead, he left it as it was, where there's no defense expert testifying to why the lack of brain infarction is not important in the cocaine drug overdose case. And the state jumped on it. They utilized it to completely gut the defense and say, well, look, if this was a drug overdose case, why didn't they look at the slides? Why didn't they look for brain infarction when that's the telltale sign of a cocaine overdose?

speaker: nardella
text: Counsel, I do have a question. Didn't Dr. Wright talk about brain infarction? He just didn't look at the slides. And so wasn't the argument being made that his testimony didn't have as much impact because he didn't emphasize that point as much as he should have?

text: Dr. Wright never mentioned brain tissue infarction. The court can look at his testimony. I cited to you the transcripts in which he testified. That never mentioned it a single time. Control find, looking through all the testimony, no testimony. An easier way for this court to look at whether Dr. Wright testified to brain tissue infarction is by looking at the state's closing arguments in this case, when they specifically highlight themselves. text: I'm going to butcher his name, Dr. Maronucci testified to that? I have his testimony.

text: Correct. When he testified as to what Dr. Wright said, he said, and did you review the testimony of Dr. Wright, who is the defense examiner as well? Yes. And Dr. Wright ever mentioned infarction in his testimony. And he says he mentioned it in his testimony. The problem I have with Dr. Wright is in my mind, he did not emphasize appropriately how rare it is to get brain infarction with cocaine intoxication.

speaker: matthewmclain
text: Well, I think Dr. Maronucci was mistaken in that testimony. And I followed up with a question at the evidentiary hearing with the record would speak for itself. And the record does speak for itself in the fact that at no point in time did Dr. Wright mention the word infarction or discussed brain infarction. So to the extent that Dr. Maronucci did say that, that that was a misstatement on his part. And the court reviews that the record and the transcripts, which Dr. Wright testified to, it will not find the word infarction. It'll talk about ischemic changes in the brain, which Dr. Kaiser talked about, that would be something that would be present in a manual strangulation case. But he just, he did discuss ischemic changes, but never the word infarction. And so in such a technical medical intense case, to not mention the actual verbiage used, which are two different things from my understanding, ischemic changes versus brain infarction. It did not refute it. And so that's where we have an issue with the court's order in this case is that the court essentially concluded after the evidentiary hearing that both Dr. Wright and Maronucci testified to the same thing and that that's simply not the case. speaker: randwallis
text: Mr. McClain wasn't, I'm sorry, you can go ahead and you finish your answer.

speaker: randwallis
text: Mr. McClain, I believe that evidence established that there was significant medical evidence or documentation as far as exterior injuries on Ms. Brevik. Is that correct?

speaker: matthewmclain
text: That is correct.

speaker: randwallis
text: Okay. And did any of the experts comment as to whether or not the location of those injuries exteriorly to on Ms. Brevik either discounted or affirmed or supported your theory of the case that she fell as a result of the brain infarction and that resulted in her hitting her head on the bedside table?

speaker: matthewmclain
text: So the external injuries to Ms. Brevik include scratch marks on her neck, bruise on her head, and several other bruises on her knees and other body parts. And Dr. Wright did testify and I believe Dr. Bonfiglio for the defense testified that these injuries could be consistent with the grand mal seizure, which was the defense theory in the case. So as far as the scratches go, there was DNA taken from the fingernails of Mr. Brevik to compare as to his wife's and there was no DNA evidence for that. The experts testified that that could have been consistent with Ms. Brevik scratching herself. And there was also evidence that she was moved by paramedics. She was given CPR. There's evidence about her eyes and the evidence related to her eyes not being consistent with manual strangulation. So there's certainly dispute from the defense side as to these physical injuries being inconsistent with manual strangulation and being consistent with grand mal seizures. Turning to the third issue, which is related to the nightstand, the nightstand was discussed by Dr. Wright as a hypothesis. Basically, the victim, Mrs. Brevik, had a fractured cornea, which is in the neck area. I guess there's two of them bilateral and only one of them was fractured. The state experts heavily relied on the fractured cornea to support its theory that this was a manual strangulation case. What Dr. Wright said was, in passing, this fracture could have occurred through any sort of blunt force. It could have been caused by the bed, it could have been caused by the nightstand, it could have been caused by many things. What we submit and what defense counsel recognized at the evidentiary hearing of board certified attorneys is that it should have been taken one step further and actually confirmed whether this was a valid hypothesis. There's simply no testing as to this theory that was presented to the jury, and therefore the state was able to attack it and state that nothing on the nightstand could have caused these injuries, when that's not true. The court went ahead and discounted the test performed by Dr. Marichini and testified to about at the evidentiary hearing. There's no support for discounting Dr. Marichini's test. The state knew that he was testifying to this test that he performed. They called no experts to refute it. I provided the case of Tyndale, which was recently decided by the fourth DCA in support of it. For the court to go ahead and insert its own beliefs as to why the test was invalid is improper under the case law. The only other issue is the first issue, which talks about the statement made by first responding officer as to the victim looking to be obviously strangled. Defense counsel did not timely object to this or request a redaction, even though it was required of him. That was very prejudicial testimony. We look at the case in totality, yes, the defense attorneys were working on a self-imposed timeline because Mr. Brevik is not the one who asserted his speedy trial demand. That was a defense counsel strategy. They did retain multiple experts for him, but they failed in critical ways that deprived Mr. Brevik of a fair trial. So we're asking the court to reverse and remand for a new trial and reserve the remaining time for rebuttal.

But it's not every cocaine overdose. text: May it please the court. To combat the state's point, you look at their closing argument as to brain tissue infarction. Dr. Wright never even looked. He told you, I didn't take any slides. Why didn't they want to look? I don't know how you can square that with the claim of ineffective assistance of counsel. Therefore, it could not be a drug overdose. Not a single expert presented by the defense talked about that. That's recognized by the defense counsel at the evidentiary hearing. He talked about, it was important testimony. I should have had an expert to talk about it. I didn't. He made some testimony about a discovery violation possibly occurring. But the record reveals he took no remedial action because of that violation. So based off of the arguments presented today, and the arguments presented in the briefing, we'd ask the court to grant Mr. Brevik a new trial and allow him to tell the jury, at least dispute the issue as to brain tissue infarction, present additional evidence as to the nightstand, and for the jury not to be tainted by the first responding officer stating that the victim had obviously been strangled. If there are no further questions, we'll rest on the brief.

speaker: randwallis
